The loss is $2.85 billion of non-refundable advances plus $0.88 billion of contract modifications and settlements, or 39.3% of cash paid.

The live risk is SB7's remaining $6.6 billion of advances. SoftBank's 12 November slide schedules $3.4 billion for recovery from PORTS-Pike in the near term, $2.2 billion by the end of 2027 and $1.0 billion over time. The timetable is management's intention, not cash returned, and it rests on project lenders.

Conditional rebates of up to $2.1 billion over ten years carry no recognised asset. If every dollar arrives, nominal cost is $1.63 billion. With none, it stays $3.73 billion.

author: Joris Kersten, MSc
headline: I sell & buy companies @ The Netherlands
text:
With M&A deals in The Netherlands, where the tax authorities, or legal issues, are involved, one focusses at “fair market value” (waarde in economisch verkeer/ WEV).

In most cases (not all) the main focus is on DCF valuation.

Although I am also a big fan of DCF, I have learned while working for the top “bulge bracket” Investment Banks in New York, London & Hong Kong during 2016-2020 that valuation should be seen much broader !

So I always argue in favour of building the whole valuation spectrum:

-LBO analysis for IRR and credit stats
-M&A analysis for EPS accretion dilution and credit stats
-Precedent deals multiples
-Comparable companies multiples
-ROIC WACC spreads adjusted for services companies (asset light)
-Adjusted net debt analysis
-DCF analysis

In my opinion, only this way one gets a good understanding of value ! Unfortunately I often see very poor cases in my home country when the focus is on DCF.

author: Tammam Al-Dandachi
headline: Executive Director | Infrastructure Investments | Public Private Partnerships
text:
At the 6th PPP MENA Forum, one discussion stayed with me. Some procurers are now looking at putting clinical services inside hospital PPPs, so that the same private partner builds the hospital and runs the clinic. Others prefer to keep the two apart.
It's a fair debate. But I think we often start it in the wrong place.

The first question isn't "integrated or separate?" It's "what problem are we trying to solve?"

Saudi Arabia is working on two problems at the same time.
The first is capacity. The national target of 27 beds per 10,000 people, against 23.4 in 2024, implies more than 21,000 additional beds by 2030, according to BSF Capital's June 2026 sector report. The same report puts the private sector at around 25% of beds, against an ambition of 45% by 2030.
The second is performance. Under the Health Sector Transformation Program, the Ministry of Health is becoming the regulator, rather than the service provider. Alongside this, selected existing hospitals and primary care centres are being opened up to private operators to get more out of what is already there.

From a distance these look like the same challenge. Up close, they carry very different risks.

A hospital building is a long, predictable asset. Once it's built, the job is to keep it available and well maintained for 25 to 30 years. That suits long-term infrastructure investors and project lenders, who can fund it efficiently because the payment stream is stable.

If you are opening in Dubai, decide which structure you want before the licence is issued rather than after.

text:
SAUDI ARABIA HAS A TWO TRILLION DOLLAR PIPELINE. ITS BANKS ARE ALREADY LENDING MORE THAN THEY HOLD.

If you are developing a hotel, a mixed-use scheme or an energy asset in the GCC, the question is no longer whether the project makes sense. It is whether your bank still has the balance sheet to fund it.

Knight Frank puts Saudi Arabia's project pipeline at USD 2.07 trillion in H1 2026, of which USD 1.23 trillion is construction and real estate, including more than 358,000 planned hotel keys through 2035. Knight Frank itself notes that some projects may need rephasing to stay commercially feasible.

The funding side is moving the other way. Fitch Ratings reports that Saudi bank credit grew 7% year on year to SAR 3.5 trillion in September, while deposits grew around 5%. The loan-to-deposit ratio has risen to around 114%, and Fitch expects funding costs to stay elevated over the next several years. #ProjectFinance

Our view: the Gulf does not have a demand problem. It has a funding sequence problem. Senior banks will keep lending, but selectively. Sponsors who need to start construction, bridge to stabilisation or refinance a maturing facility will increasingly have to assemble the capital stack themselves: senior debt, a mezzanine layer, a bridge loan and family office capital that understands the asset. #PrivateCredit is moving from alternative to necessity.

The Rise of Specialized Investment Funds & Joint Ventures in KSA’s Real Estate and Infrastructure Ecosystem
Saudi Arabia’s investment landscape is evolving. The challenge is no longer simply finding capital, but structuring it effectively.
Alongside traditional corporate debt, investors are increasingly exploring:
·        Specialized real estate and infrastructure funds.
·        Private equity and private capital platforms.
·        Greenfield infrastructure funds.
·        Strategic Joint Ventures (JVs).
·        PPP and hybrid financing structures.
These structures combine capital, assets, expertise and operational capabilities while allocating risks more effectively.
What attracts institutional investors?
An attractive project is not automatically an investable proposition. Three disciplines are essential:
1. Robust financial modelling
Integrating CAPEX, funding structures, debt capacity, cash flows, equity returns and investor distributions.
2. Sensitivity analysis and risk allocation
Testing exposure to cost overruns, delays, interest rates, occupancy, operating costs, refinancing and exit valuations.
3. Credible exit strategies
Establishing realistic routes to liquidity through asset sales, refinancing, portfolio aggregation, acquisitions or secondary transactions.
Where is the advisory opportunity?
This evolving market creates demand for senior financial and transaction advisory expertise.

text:
Part 2/4 · B&M Finance & GCC Readiness Series

Why do strong B.Com, M.Com, and semi-qualified finance graduates get filtered out in Global Capability Centre (GCC) and US/UK KPO interviews across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram, and Chennai?

Hiring managers rarely stop at textbook definitions — they test four applied workflow differences:

1. Revenue Collectability (ASC 606 vs IFRS 15)
Both frameworks share the 5-step model, yet US GAAP ASC 606 interprets "probable" collectability at roughly 75–80%, higher than IFRS 15's "more likely than not" (>50%) bar.

2. Lessee Accounting (ASC 842 vs IFRS 16)
US GAAP preserves a dual lessee model (operating vs finance leases with straight-line vs front-loaded P&L recognition), whereas IFRS 16 puts nearly all leases onto a single lessee model.

3. 5-Day Month-End Close & 3-Way Reconciliations
Interviewers hand you raw CSV sub-ledgers and test prepaid schedules, accrued expenses, FX revaluation, and bank-to-GL reconciliations under tight close timelines.

4. Cloud Accounting Stack (QuickBooks Online, Xero, NetSuite)
Hands-on multi-currency AP/AR and close navigation matters far more than passive certificates.

Save this post for your interview prep, and follow B&M Global Solutions for Part 3/4 (SQL & Power BI interview checks).

author: Michael Calver
headline: Bringing products to market that help people make better decisions faster, and helping founders get the big ones right.
text:
Winning an Innovate UK grant doesn't put cash in the bank. Not for months. 💷

Grants are paid quarterly in arrears. You spend first, claim after each quarter ends, and Innovate UK normally pays within 30 days of the claim. It also holds back 10% of the grant until your final claim and report are in.

A real timeline from this year's Growth Catalyst round. 📅

🔹 Deadline 3 February
🔹 Applicants told 17 March
🔹 Projects start 1 July
🔹 First quarter ends 30 September

The first payment lands roughly eight to ten months after the deadline.

Three things to plan for.

1. Fund at least two quarters of project costs before the first claim is paid
2. Only claim what you've already paid for, with a narrow exception in the final quarter
3. Budget for the independent accountant's report that larger grants need with some claims

A grant is still some of the best money a deep tech company can get. Just don't treat the offer letter as cash.

How did you bridge the gap on your first grant?

Saudi-listed Acwa, one of the world's largest independent power producers, has signed a definitive agreement with institutional investor EIG to create Plenum Power, a strategic partnership aimed at energy and infrastructure investment opportunities in the United States.

The parties intend to launch the platform with an initial equity commitment of approximately US$4 billion. The deal marks Acwa's entry into the US market.

WHAT THE PARTNERSHIP DOES
Plenum Power will combine two complementary sets of skills. Acwa brings its global capability in developing, financing, constructing and operating large-scale infrastructure across conventional and renewable power generation and energy storage, along with a track record of delivering projects at scale, driving down energy costs and maintaining strong operational performance. EIG contributes its experience in sourcing, establishing, financing and scaling energy infrastructure platforms.

In practical terms, this is a platform joint venture: rather than buying a single asset, the two partners are pooling capital and expertise into a vehicle that can originate and fund a pipeline of US power and infrastructure projects over time. That structure lets the partners share development risk and deploy capital repeatedly without renegotiating a new deal for every project.

author: Sara Anjum
headline: Deeptech VC | Semiconductors, Advanced Materials, Energy, Physical AI
text:
As someone in the early-stage deeptech space, much of what I encounter and diligence regularly is B2B technology. D2C consumer deeptech DOES exist, but I'm rather skeptical of much of it outside of the personal health space. 

Even in the personal health space, some of it leaves me skeptical. Especially (though this might partly be my bias and principles having been an investor) the devices for which I get Instagram ads that are effectively crowdfunding their devices but provide no equity upside to us early consumer supporters  😂 

I know equity crowdfunding can have its downsides in signaling, but some have yielded notable success and exits: 

• Revolut raised 1 million British pounds from 433 investors through Crowdcube in 2016. It's currently valued at $115B and is targeting a 2028 IPO
• JUMP Bikes was acquired by Uber
• Jayride had an IPO and listed on Australia's exchange
• Replit raised money on Wefunder AFTER receiving institutional investment from notable firms like Andreessen Horowitz before crowdfunding

Even medical devices and pharmaceuticals have seen equity crowdfunding successes, such as:

• Beta Bionics: an automated bionic pancreas system, raised $1M from 718 investors on WeFunder in 2016, the first day regulation crowdfunding became available to non-accredited investors, and eventually IPOed in 2025

• CNS Pharmaceuticals, Inc. raised over $600k on Republic in 2018 before its IPO in 2019

So my question is: when should companies consider equity crowdfunding

author: Nima Amini
headline: Commercial Real Estate & Hotel Investments | Debt & Equity Advisory | Managing Partner, Multi-Family Office | Commodity Trading | GCC · Euro
text:
SAUDI ARABIA HAS A TWO TRILLION DOLLAR PIPELINE. ITS BANKS ARE ALREADY LENDING MORE THAN THEY HOLD.

If you are developing a hotel, a mixed-use scheme or an energy asset in the GCC, the question is no longer whether the project makes sense. It is whether your bank still has the balance sheet to fund it.

Knight Frank puts Saudi Arabia's project pipeline at USD 2.07 trillion in H1 2026, of which USD 1.23 trillion is construction and real estate, including more than 358,000 planned hotel keys through 2035. Knight Frank itself notes that some projects may need rephasing to stay commercially feasible.

The funding side is moving the other way. Fitch Ratings reports that Saudi bank credit grew 7% year on year to SAR 3.5 trillion in September, while deposits grew around 5%. The loan-to-deposit ratio has risen to around 114%, and Fitch expects funding costs to stay elevated over the next several years. #ProjectFinance

Our view: the Gulf does not have a demand problem. It has a funding sequence problem. Senior banks will keep lending, but selectively. Sponsors who need to start construction, bridge to stabilisation or refinance a maturing facility will increasingly have to assemble the capital stack themselves: senior debt, a mezzanine layer, a bridge loan and family office capital that understands the asset. #PrivateCredit is moving from alternative to necessity.
